mainTopic: Aggadic teachings on curses, the desert complaints about fish, and the wonders of the מן
overview: This amud is full of אגדה. It opens by finishing a מחלוקת of רבי אמי and רבי אסי about a heavy drinker, then brings their views on dealing with worry and on the snake eating dust. A ברייתא of רבי יוסי then teaches that every curse from הקדוש ברוך הוא still has kindness inside it: the snake, כנען, the woman, and the ground. Next, רב and שמואל argue whether בני ישראל in the desert missed real fish from מצרים or relationships that the תורה later forbade. The גמרא tests both views against several פסוקים and ends with 'both happened.' The rest of the amud describes the מן: the foods it could not taste like, its shape and color, and three readings of the word גד. Several ברייתות teach that the מן revealed hidden truths in court cases, and that where it fell and how ready it was depended on a person's righteousness. Perfumes, spices, and precious stones fell with it, and it had many flavors. The amud ends with רבי יהושע בן קרחה's teaching that meat asked for improperly was given improperly; his contrast with the bread continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the dispute about the habitual drinker
steps.stepSummary: The two views of רבי אמי and רבי אסי conclude. One says a drunkard sees all עריות as permitted. The other says he sees everything in the world as permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: [One said: whoever casts] his eye on his cup, all forbidden relationships look to him like flat, smooth ground. And the other said: whoever casts his eye on his cup, the whole world looks to him like flat, smooth ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an argument that started on the previous amud. Two אמוראים explain the word 'מישרים' in the פסוק about wine: what does a heavy drinker stop noticing?
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Level ground' means he no longer sees the danger or the 'bumps' of sin. The first view limits this to עריות. The second view goes further: every איסור in the world, including money matters, seems permitted to him.

keyTerms.meaning: Casts his eye on his cup, meaning someone who is always focused on drinking
Flat, level ground; here it means that sin looks easy and harmless
And the other one said, introducing the second view in a dispute

steps.confusionAlert: This amud starts in the middle of a sentence. The words 'כל הנותן' and the names of the two אמוראים, רבי אמי and רבי אסי, came on the previous עמוד.

phrases.english: [whoever casts] his eye on his cup,
phrases.notes: Continuation of the first opinion from the previous עמוד

phrases.english: all forbidden relationships look to him like level ground.

phrases.aramaic: וְחַד אָמַר: כָּל הַנּוֹתֵן עֵינוֹ בְּכוֹסוֹ,
phrases.english: And one said: whoever casts his eye on his cup,

phrases.aramaic: כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ דּוֹמֶה עָלָיו כְּמִישׁוֹר.
phrases.english: the whole world looks to him like level ground.
phrases.notes: All איסורים seem permitted, not only עריות

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחַד אָמַר: כָּל הַנּוֹתֵן עֵינוֹ בְּכוֹסוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a dispute begun on the previous amud
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Habitual drinking makes sin look harmless. One view says this applies to עריות; the other says it applies to everything.

steps.title: How to deal with worry in the heart
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי and רבי אסי read the word 'ישחנה' in a פסוק in משלי in two ways. Either push the worry out of your mind, or talk it over with others.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Worry in a man's heart, let him ישחנה.' רבי אמי and רבי אסי disagree. One said: let him push it out of his mind. And one said: let him talk about it to others.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new פסוק, and the same two אמוראים argue about what one word means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'ישחנה' can be read as 'יַשִּׂחֶנָּה,' meaning push it away, or as 'יְשִׂיחֶנָּה,' meaning speak it out. Both readings give advice for worry: either clear it from your thoughts or share it so it feels lighter.

keyTerms.meaning: He should push it out of his mind
He should tell it to others

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known piece of Torah advice. Both approaches to handling worry are drawn from one word in the פסוק.

phrases.english: 'If there is worry in a man's heart, let him quash it' (Proverbs 12:25),
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi [disagree]:
One said: he should push it out of his mind,
and one said: he should tell it to others.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new פסוק explained by the same pair of אמוראים
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Deal with worry either by pushing it out of your mind or by sharing it with others.

steps.title: What it means that the snake eats dust
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי and רבי אסי explain 'ונחש עפר לחמו' in two ways. Either all food tastes like dust to the snake, or it is never satisfied until it also eats dust.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And dust shall be the snake's food.' רבי אמי and רבי אסי disagree. One said: even if it eats all the delicacies in the world, they taste like dust to it. And one said: even if it eats all the delicacies in the world, it is not settled until it eats dust.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third פסוק, and the same two אמוראים give two explanations of the snake's curse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both views agree that the snake can eat fine food. They disagree about what the curse does. In the first view, all food tastes like dust to it. In the second view, the snake still needs dust to feel satisfied.

keyTerms.meaning: All the delicacies of the world
It is not calm or satisfied

phrases.english: 'And dust shall be the snake's food' (Isaiah 65:25),
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi [disagree]:

phrases.aramaic: חַד אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ אוֹכֵל כָּל מַעֲדַנֵּי עוֹלָם —
phrases.english: One said: even if it eats all the delicacies of the world,
it tastes in them the taste of dust,

phrases.aramaic: וְחַד אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ אוֹכֵל כׇּל מַעֲדַנֵּי עוֹלָם —
phrases.english: and one said: even if it eats all the delicacies of the world,
it is not satisfied
until it eats dust.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third פסוק explained by the same pair of אמוראים
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The snake's curse means either that all food tastes like dust to it, or that it is not satisfied without dust.

steps.title: How people treat someone they want to hurt
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא of רבי יוסי begins with a contrast. When a human wants to provoke someone, he goes after that person's whole life.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי יוסי said: Come and see that the way of flesh and blood is not like the way of הקדוש ברוך הוא. The way of flesh and blood is this: when one provokes his fellow, he goes after him for his very livelihood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא connected to the snake topic. This step sets up a contrast, describing human behavior so that the next step can show how הקב״ה is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a person is angry at someone, he tries to damage that person's life and livelihood. This human pattern is the background for the next step, which shows what הקב״ה did with the snake.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
Goes after his very life and livelihood

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yosei said:
Come and see

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא כְּמִדַּת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִדַּת בָּשָׂר וָדָם.
phrases.english: that the way of flesh and blood is not like the way of the Holy One, Blessed be He.
The way of flesh and blood:

phrases.aramaic: מַקְנִיט אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ — יוֹרֵד עִמּוֹ לְחַיָּיו.
phrases.english: one who provokes his fellow goes after his very livelihood.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: בּוֹא וּרְאֵה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A ברייתא that continues the topic of the snake's curse
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Humans who are angry attack the other person's livelihood.

steps.title: The snake's curse still gives it food everywhere
steps.stepSummary: הקב״ה is different. Even when He cursed the snake, its food, dust, is wherever it goes.
steps.simpleTranslation: But הקדוש ברוך הוא is not like that. He cursed the snake, yet when it goes up to the roof its food is with it, and when it goes down below its food is with it.
steps.whatsHappening: This step finishes רבי יוסי's contrast. Even in a curse, הקב״ה made sure the snake would always have food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dust is everywhere, so the snake never lacks food. A human who punishes someone tries to cut off his livelihood. הקב״ה's curse actually left the snake with food wherever it goes.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוסי teaches that even when הקב״ה punishes, He does not destroy the livelihood of the one being punished. The snake's 'dust' curse means its food is everywhere.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as saying the snake was not cursed. It was truly cursed. The point is that even inside the curse, its food was still provided.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֵינוֹ כֵּן:
phrases.english: But the Holy One, Blessed be He, is not so:
He cursed the snake,
when it goes up to the roof, its food is with it,
when it goes down below, its food is with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֵינוֹ כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the contrast that step 4 set up
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even in a curse, הקב״ה provided the snake with food wherever it goes.

steps.title: Every curse of הקב״ה has a blessing inside it
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי's ברייתא continues with three more examples: כנען, the woman, and the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: He cursed כנען, yet the slave eats what his master eats and drinks what his master drinks. He cursed the woman, yet everyone runs after her. He cursed the ground, yet everyone is fed from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא of רבי יוסי adds three more examples to the snake example from the last step. Each curse from הקב״ה still holds something good.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כנען was cursed to be a slave, but a slave does not have to worry about his food. The woman was cursed, yet she is still wanted and sought after for marriage. The ground was cursed after אדם's sin, yet it still feeds the whole world.

keyTerms.meaning: Canaan, who was cursed to be a slave

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוסי's point: a person who curses goes after his victim's whole life, but every curse from הקב״ה still has mercy built into it.

phrases.english: He cursed Canaan,
phrases.notes: כנען was cursed to be a slave (בראשית 9:25).

phrases.english: yet he eats what his master eats
and drinks what his master drinks.

phrases.aramaic: קִלֵּל אֶת הָאִשָּׁה — הַכֹּל רָצִין אַחֲרֶיהָ.
phrases.english: He cursed the woman, yet everyone runs after her.

phrases.aramaic: קִלֵּל אֶת הָאֲדָמָה — הַכֹּל נִיזּוֹנִין הֵימֶנָּה.
phrases.english: He cursed the ground, yet everyone is fed from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues and finishes רבי יוסי's list of examples that began with the snake.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every curse of הקב״ה holds a hidden benefit.

steps.title: What did they miss from מצרים: fish or forbidden relationships?
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל argue about what 'הדגה' means in the פסוק 'זכרנו את הדגה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'We remember the fish that we ate in מצרים for free.' רב and שמואל disagree. One says it means real fish. The other says it means עריות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes the complaint of בני ישראל in the desert, and two אמוראים argue about what it means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One view reads the פסוק simply: they missed real fish. The other view says 'fish' is a hidden way of describing relationships that were allowed in מצרים but became forbidden once the תורה was given.

phrases.english: "We remember the fish
that we ate in Egypt for free",
Rav and Shmuel disagree:
one said: real fish,
and one said: forbidden relationships.

steps.triggerLanguage: זָכַרְנוּ אֶת הַדָּגָה אֲשֶׁר נֹאכַל בְּמִצְרַיִם חִנָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. It ties loosely to the earlier talk about food and עריות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a מחלוקת whether 'הדגה' means fish or עריות.

steps.title: Which word each side builds on
steps.stepSummary: The fish view builds on the word 'נאכל'. The עריות view builds on the word 'חנם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says fish relies on the word 'we ate'. The one who says עריות relies on the word 'for free'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows which word in the פסוק supports each side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'We ate' sounds like real food, so it supports fish. 'For free' supports עריות, because the מצרים would never have given slaves free fish. What was 'free' was freedom from the מצוות, since the forbidden relationships had not yet been banned.

phrases.english: The one who says fish: because it is written "we ate."
And the one who says forbidden relationships: because it is written "for free."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source in the פסוק for each side of the מחלוקת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each view rests on a different word in the פסוק.

steps.title: Challenge to the עריות view from the word 'we ate'
steps.stepSummary: If the פסוק means עריות, why does it say 'we ate'?
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says עריות, the פסוק says 'we ate'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the עריות view with the word the fish view relies on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Eating' sounds like real food. So how can the פסוק be talking about relationships?

keyTerms.meaning: and according to the one who says

phrases.english: And according to the one who says forbidden relationships,
but it is written "we ate"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the fish view's source against the עריות view.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'נאכל' points to real eating, not to relationships.

steps.title: 'Eating' is a polite word for relations
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק used a clean expression. We see this in משלי, where 'eating' describes an adulterous woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק used a refined way of speaking, as it is written: 'She ate, wiped her mouth, and said: I did nothing wrong.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'eating' can be a modest way of saying intimacy, and brings a proof from משלי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה avoids crude words. A פסוק in משלי uses 'eating' to describe the adulterous woman, so 'נאכל' fits the עריות view.

phrases.english: It used a refined expression,
as it is written: "She ate and wiped her mouth
and said: I have done no wrong."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against the עריות view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the word as a euphemism
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Eating' is a modest way of saying relations, as in משלי.

steps.title: Challenge to the fish view from the word 'for free'
steps.stepSummary: If the פסוק means real fish, what does 'free' mean?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the one who says fish, what does 'for free' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא challenges the fish view with the word the עריות view relies on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצרים worked the Jews as slaves and would never have handed them free food. So how could the fish have been free?

phrases.english: And according to the one who says fish,
what is "for free"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A mirror-image challenge, aimed at the other view.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Slaves in מצרים would not get free fish.

steps.title: The fish came from ownerless water
steps.stepSummary: The fish were free because they came from הפקר. הקב״ה sent small fish into their water jugs.
steps.simpleTranslation: They took the fish from ownerless property. As the master said: when ישראל drew water, הקב״ה prepared small fish for them inside the water, in their jugs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the fish really were free. They did not come from the מצרים but from the river, which belonged to no one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Free' does not mean the מצרים gave the fish. The fish came from הפקר. A teaching is brought that small fish would swim right into the Jews' water jugs, a gift from הקב״ה.

phrases.english: For they would bring them from ownerless property.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר מָר: כְּשֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל שׁוֹאֲבִין מַיִם,
phrases.english: As the master said: when Israel would draw water,
the Holy One, Blessed be He, would provide for them
small fish inside the water, in their jugs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against the fish view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining how the case actually happened
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Free' would mean the מצרים gave fish away, which is impossible.
steps.terutzMaskana: The fish were free because they came from הפקר and swam into their jugs.

steps.title: 'A locked garden' fits the fish view
steps.stepSummary: For the fish view, the פסוק praising the Jews' modesty in מצרים fits easily.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the one who says fish: they were not loose with עריות. That is why it is written: 'A locked garden is my sister, the bride...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It shows that the fish view fits a פסוק in שיר השירים, which prepares a question on the עריות view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שיר השירים praises the Jews for being 'locked' and 'sealed', meaning they kept away from immorality. If they missed only fish, they were never loose with relationships, so the praise fits perfectly. The 'גו׳' points to the rest of the פסוק: 'גל נעול מעין חתום', 'a locked spring, a sealed fountain'.
steps.confusionAlert: 'גו׳' means 'etc.' The גמרא is about to ask on the next words of the same פסוק, 'מעין חתום', which do not appear here.

phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who says fish,
but they were not loose with forbidden relationships,
this is what is written:
"A locked garden is my sister, the bride, etc."
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 4:12. It continues: 'a locked spring, a sealed fountain.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a בשלמא...אלא structure that tests both views against a new פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The fish view easily fits the praise of the Jews' modesty.

steps.title: How does 'a sealed fountain' fit the עריות view?
steps.stepSummary: If the Jews wanted forbidden relationships, how can they be praised as a 'sealed fountain'?
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to the one who says עריות, what does 'a sealed fountain' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: Here is the challenge that the last step set up, now aimed at the עריות view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If בני ישראל cried over losing relationships, that seems to show they were not modest. So how can the פסוק praise them as sealed?

phrases.english: But according to the one who says forbidden relationships,
what is "a sealed fountain"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר עֲרָיוֹת, מַאי מַעְיָן חָתוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the בשלמא structure with a challenge.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Missing forbidden relationships seems to clash with being praised as modest.

steps.title: They were careful with what was already forbidden
steps.stepSummary: They kept away from relationships that were already forbidden, and missed only the ones the תורה added later.
steps.simpleTranslation: From those that were already forbidden, they were not loose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the praise is real. In מצרים, the Jews kept away from every relationship that was already forbidden to them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In מצרים they kept the עריות that were already forbidden, such as those in the שבע מצוות בני נח. What they cried over in the desert were the new bans added at מתן תורה. So the 'sealed fountain' praise is still true.
steps.whatToRemember: Both views work. Fish: they missed free fish from the river. עריות: they missed relationships that became forbidden only at מתן תורה, while they had always kept the ones already forbidden.

phrases.english: With those that were already forbidden, they were not loose.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge, so the עריות view stays standing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the scope of the praise
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Missing עריות means they were never modest.
steps.terutzMaskana: They were modest about what was already forbidden. They missed only the new bans from מתן תורה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both readings of 'הדגה' fit the פסוקים.

steps.title: The verse 'weeping for their families' fits only the forbidden-relationships view
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says the people cried 'for their families.' That fits the view that they cried over עריות. How does it fit the view that they cried over fish?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for the one who says they cried about forbidden relationships, because the פסוק says 'משה heard the people weeping for their families,' meaning about their family members whom they were now forbidden to live with. But for the one who says they cried about fish, what does 'weeping for their families' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another פסוק that seems to support the עריות view and challenges the fish view with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'for their families' sound like the crying was about family relationships. That fits the עריות view perfectly. For the fish view, these words seem to have no meaning, so the fish view is under attack.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted / it makes sense (sets up a contrast with a view that has a problem)

phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who said forbidden relationships,
this is what is written:
"And Moshe heard the people
weeping for their families",
about matters of their families,
phrases.notes: Read as: about their family members

phrases.english: that it became forbidden for them to lie with them.
But according to the one who said fish,
what is "weeping for their families"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the עריות view survived the 'sealed fountain' challenge (steps 13–15), the גמרא reverses the בשלמא...אלא structure and tests the fish view against another פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that the Jews cried over fish
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The phrase 'for their families' points to family relationships; the fish view leaves it unexplained.

steps.title: Both things happened
steps.stepSummary: The people cried about both: the fish and the forbidden relationships.
steps.simpleTranslation: This and that both happened.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there is no contradiction: the people cried about fish and also about the new forbidden relationships.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fish view does not need to deny the crying over עריות. One פסוק describes crying over fish, and 'for their families' describes crying over relationships. Both complaints were real.
steps.whatToRemember: The final answer is that the Jews cried about both the fish of מצרים and the new laws of עריות.

phrases.english: This and that both happened.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Combining both views: both reasons for crying are true
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two views exclude each other, so the fish view cannot explain 'for their families.'
steps.terutzMaskana: Both kinds of crying happened, so each פסוק refers to a different complaint.

steps.title: Why they missed the five foods if the מן tasted like everything
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי and רבי אסי argue. One says the מן could taste like any food except these five. The other says these five gave only taste but not the feeling of the real food.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The cucumbers and the melons': רבי אמי and רבי אסי argue. One said: they could taste every kind of food in the מן, but they could not taste these five foods in it. The other said: with every food they tasted both its taste and its substance, but with these five they got only the taste, not the substance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to another phrase in the same פסוק and brings a מחלוקת explaining why the people missed cucumbers, melons and other foods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the מן could taste like anything, it is strange that the people missed these foods. One view says these five tastes were simply missing from the מן. The other view says the taste was there, but not the real feeling and texture of eating them.

keyTerms.meaning: The food that fell from heaven in the desert

steps.confusionAlert: The two views do not argue about whether the מן had many tastes. Both agree it did. They argue only about what was missing with these five foods: the whole taste, or just the texture.

phrases.english: "The cucumbers and the melons",
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi argue:

phrases.aramaic: חַד אָמַר: טַעַם כׇּל הַמִּינִין טָעֲמוּ בַּמָּן,
phrases.english: One said: they tasted the taste of all kinds of food in the manna,

phrases.aramaic: טַעַם חֲמֵשֶׁת הַמִּינִין הַלָּלוּ לֹא טָעֲמוּ בּוֹ,
phrases.english: but the taste of these five kinds they did not taste in it,

phrases.aramaic: וְחַד אָמַר: טַעַם כָּל הַמִּינִין טָעֲמוּ טַעְמָן וּמַמָּשָׁן,
phrases.english: and one said: with all kinds of food they tasted their taste and their substance,
but these, their taste and not their substance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the same פסוק about what the people remembered from מצרים, now explaining the vegetables.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two views: either the five foods' taste was missing from the מן, or only their texture was missing.

steps.title: The מן was round like coriander and white like a pearl
steps.stepSummary: Coriander is not white, so רבי אסי explains that the comparison is to its round shape. The whiteness was like a pearl.
steps.simpleTranslation: '(And the מן was) like coriander seed, white (and its taste...).' רבי אסי said: round like coriander, and white like a pearl.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains a פסוק describing the מן, and רבי אסי splits the comparison into two parts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק seems to say the מן was white like coriander, but coriander seeds are not white. רבי אסי reads it as two separate comparisons: the shape is like coriander, and the color is white like a pearl.

phrases.english: "(And the manna) was like coriander seed, white (and its taste...)".
Rabbi Asi said: round like coriander
and white like a pearl.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues describing the מן, now its look rather than its taste.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מן had coriander's round shape and a pearl's white color.

steps.title: A ברייתא also compares גד to a seed's shape
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports the idea that גד describes shape, comparing it to flax seeds on their stalks.
steps.simpleTranslation: (This was also taught:) גד, because it looks like flax seed on its stalks.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that also explains גד by what it looks like, backing up רבי אסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא explains the word גד as a comparison to the look of flax seeds bunched on their stalks. This supports reading גד as describing the shape of the מן, not its color.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא supports)

phrases.english: (It was also taught so:) Gad —
because it resembles flax seed on its stalks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי אסי's reading of גד as describing shape.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אסי's view that גד refers to the shape of the מן
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא comparing גד to flax seeds on their stalks

steps.title: גד is like הגדה, which pulls the heart like water
steps.stepSummary: Others read גד as connected to הגדה: the מן drew people's hearts the way a good story or water does.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others say: גד, because it is like הגדה, which draws a person's heart like water.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, non-literal reading of the word גד from a group called אחרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of describing the look of the מן, this view plays on the sound of גד and הגדה. Just as words of אגדה draw the heart the way water draws a thirsty person, the מן drew people to it.

phrases.english: Others say: Gad —
because it is like aggadah,
which draws a person's heart like water.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different meaning of the same word גד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גד hints that the מן attracted the heart like הגדה and like water.

steps.title: The מן told whose baby it was
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא reads גד as מגיד: the מן told Israel whether a baby was a nine-month child of the first husband or a seven-month child of the second.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא taught: גד, because it told Israel whether a baby was a nine-month baby belonging to the first husband, or a seven-month baby belonging to the second.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third meaning of גד, connecting it to the word מגיד, 'tells.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a woman remarried quickly and gave birth, it could be unclear which husband was the father. Since the מן fell for each family by its number of members, the baby's share of מן showed up at the home of the real father and settled the question.

keyTerms.meaning: A baby born after nine months
A baby born after seven months

steps.whatToRemember: The word גד is explained three ways: its shape (like a seed), its pull on the heart (like הגדה), and its power to tell (מגיד) who a baby's father was.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the מן did more than feed people. It also cleared up real doubts about הלכה, here a question of who a baby's father was.

phrases.english: Another baraita taught: Gad —
because it told Israel
whether he is a nine-month baby, belonging to the first husband,
or a seven-month baby, belonging to the second.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a third meaning of גד, after the views of shape and of הגדה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גד means מגיד: the מן revealed whether a baby belonged to the first or second husband.

steps.title: White means the מן whitened Israel's sins
steps.stepSummary: The word לבן in the description of the מן is read as a hint that the מן cleansed Israel's sins.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'White' — because it made the sins of Israel white (clean).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more reading of a word in the verse describing the מן. This time the word is לבן, 'white.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 19 the whiteness was a physical description, like a pearl. Here the same word is read in a spiritual way: the מן 'whitened' sins. The גמרא does not say how. The Steinsaltz explanation is that the people feared the מן would stop falling if they sinned, so they did תשובה and became clean.

phrases.english: 'White' —
phrases.notes: A word quoted from the verse describing the מן

phrases.english: because it whitens the sins of Israel.
phrases.notes: A wordplay: לבן (white) and מלבין (makes white)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of word-readings on the verse describing the מן, now turning from גד to לבן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word לבן hints that the מן cleansed Israel of their sins.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: the מן revealed hidden things like a prophet
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי יוסי: just as a נביא revealed hidden things to Israel, the מן did too. It ends with 'How so?' to introduce examples.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: רבי יוסי says: Just as the prophet would tell Israel what was in the holes and what was in the cracks, so the מן told Israel what was in the holes and what was in the cracks. How so?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that states a general rule: the מן revealed hidden matters. The closing word 'כיצד' sets up the examples that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This backs up the idea from step 22 that the מן was a מגיד, a 'teller' of truth. 'Holes and cracks' is a picture of things that are hidden. The concrete court cases come in the next two steps.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Yosei says:

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁהַנָּבִיא הָיָה מַגִּיד לָהֶם לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
phrases.english: Just as the prophet would tell Israel
what was in the holes and what was in the cracks,
so the manna told Israel
what was in the holes and what was in the cracks.
How so?
phrases.notes: Sets up the examples that follow

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives broader support for the idea from step 22 that the מן was a 'teller' of hidden truth.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that the מן revealed hidden truths (the מגיד reading).
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא of רבי יוסי comparing the מן to a נביא.

steps.title: The slave case: where the slave's מן falls shows who owns him
steps.stepSummary: Two people argue over a slave: one says it was stolen, the other says it was sold. משה waits until morning. The house where the slave's portion of מן falls shows the truth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two people came before משה for judgment. One said: 'You stole my slave.' The other said: 'You sold him to me.' משה said: 'In the morning there will be judgment.' The next day, if the slave's עומר of מן was found in his first master's house, it was clear the second man stole him. If it was found in his second master's house, it was clear the first man sold him.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the first example of רבי יוסי's rule. The מן settles an ownership dispute that no human witness could settle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מן fell for each person at the home of the one he truly belonged to. If the slave's portion still came to the first master, the slave still belonged to him and no sale ever happened, so the second man had stolen him. If it came to the second master, the sale was real.

keyTerms.meaning: the daily measure of מן for each person
in the morning there will be judgment
it is known / it is clear

phrases.english: Two who came before Moses for judgment,
this one says: You stole my slave,
and that one says: You sold him to me.
Moses said to them: In the morning, judgment.

phrases.aramaic: לְמָחָר, אִם נִמְצָא עוֹמְרוֹ בְּבֵית רַבּוֹ רִאשׁוֹן —
phrases.english: The next day, if his omer was found in his first master's house —
it is known that this one stole him.

phrases.aramaic: אִם נִמְצָא עוֹמְרוֹ בְּבֵית רַבּוֹ שֵׁנִי —
phrases.english: If his omer was found in his second master's house —
it is known that this one sold him to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'כיצד' of step 24 with a first example.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The location of the slave's מן reveals whether he was stolen or sold.

steps.title: The husband and wife case: where her מן falls shows who was at fault
steps.stepSummary: A husband and wife each blame the other. In the morning, if her מן falls in her husband's house, she was at fault. If it falls in her father's house, he was at fault.
steps.simpleTranslation: And similarly, a man and a woman came before משה for judgment. He says: 'She wronged me.' She says: 'He wronged me.' משה said: 'In the morning there will be judgment.' The next day, if her עומר was found in her husband's house, it was clear she wronged him. If her עומר was found in her father's house, it was clear he wronged her.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second example of רבי יוסי's rule. The מן settles a marriage dispute about who is to blame.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If her מן still came to her husband's home, he had treated her properly and still deserved to have her in his household, so the fault was hers. If it came to her father's home, the husband had lost that right, so the fault was his. Who was at fault decides whether she receives her כתובה.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read it backwards. Her מן landing in her husband's house means SHE was at fault, because it shows he was still fit to have her in his household.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אִישׁ וְאִשָּׁה שֶׁבָּאוּ לִפְנֵי מֹשֶׁה לַדִּין,
phrases.english: And similarly, a man and a woman who came before Moses for judgment,
he says: She wronged me,
and she says: He wronged me.
Moses said to them: In the morning, judgment.

phrases.aramaic: לְמָחָר, אִם נִמְצָא עוֹמְרָהּ בְּבֵית בַּעְלָהּ —
phrases.english: The next day, if her omer was found in her husband's house —
it is known that she wronged him;
if her omer was found in her father's house —
it is known that he wronged her.

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוסי's ברייתא: the מן acted like a נביא, revealing hidden truths. It settled ownership of a slave and blame in a marriage dispute.
steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן אִישׁ וְאִשָּׁה שֶׁבָּאוּ לִפְנֵי מֹשֶׁה לַדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel second example, following the same pattern as the slave case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The location of the wife's מן reveals which spouse was at fault.

steps.title: Three verses describe the falling of the מן differently
steps.stepSummary: One verse says the מן fell on the camp. Another says the people went out to gather it. A third says they wandered about to gather it. How do these fit together?
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written: 'And when the dew fell upon the camp at night, the מן fell upon it.' And it is written: 'The people shall go out and gather.' And it is written: 'The people wandered about and gathered.' How can this be?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It lines up three verses that seem to contradict each other about where the מן fell, then asks how they can all be true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first verse sounds like the מן landed right in the camp. The second sounds like people had to leave the camp. The third sounds like they had to wander far. 'הא כיצד' sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: how can this be? (asks to reconcile verses)

phrases.english: It is written: 'And when the dew fell upon the camp at night,'
'the manna fell upon it,'
phrases.notes: במדבר 11:9. Here the מן lands on the camp itself.

phrases.english: and it is written: 'The people shall go out and gather,'
phrases.notes: שמות 16:4. Here people go out to gather it.

phrases.english: and it is written: 'The people wandered about and gathered,'
How can this be?

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּתִיב: ״וּבְרֶדֶת הַטַּל עַל הַמַּחֲנֶה לָיְלָה״, וּכְתִיב: ״וְיָצָא הָעָם וְלָקְטוּ״, וּכְתִיב: ״שָׁטוּ הָעָם וְלָקְטוּ״, הָא כֵּיצַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from word-readings about the מן to a contradiction between verses about how it fell.
steps.kashyaTarget: The three verses describing where the מן fell
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verses seem to disagree: the מן fell on the camp, people had to go out of the camp, and people had to wander far.

steps.title: The distance to the מן depended on a person's righteousness
steps.stepSummary: Each verse describes a different group. For צדיקים the מן fell at their door. בינונים went out to gather it. רשעים had to wander far.
steps.simpleTranslation: The righteous: it fell at the door of their homes. The average people: they went out and gathered. The wicked: they wandered about and gathered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction. All three verses are true, each about a different kind of person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse about the מן falling on the camp describes צדיקים. 'Going out' describes בינונים, and 'wandering' describes רשעים. This also explains how the מן 'whitened sins' (step 23): a person's spiritual level was visible to everyone, which pushed people to do תשובה.
steps.whatToRemember: The three verses describe three levels: צדיקים got the מן at their door, בינונים went out for it, and רשעים had to wander far.

phrases.english: The righteous: it fell at the entrance of their homes.
The average: they went out and gathered.
The wicked: they wandered about and gathered.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the verses: each verse applies to a different group of people.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The verses describe one single way the מן fell for everyone, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each verse describes a different spiritual level, so there is no contradiction.

steps.title: Three verses describe the מן differently
steps.stepSummary: The verses call the מן 'bread', 'cakes', and something that was 'ground'. How can all three be true?
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written 'bread', and it is written 'cakes', and it is written 'and they ground it'. How can this be?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out three verses that seem to describe the מן in three different ways. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Bread' means fully baked and ready. 'Cakes' means dough, not yet baked. 'Ground' means raw kernels that still needed grinding. These are three different states, so the verses seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Bread (already baked and ready to eat)
And they ground it (it came as raw grain)
How can this be? (a question about how to fit sources together)

phrases.english: It is written "bread",
and it is written "cakes,"
and it is written "and they ground it."
How can this be?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the same pattern as Steps 27–28: verses that seem to clash, then sorted by spiritual level.
steps.kashyaTarget: The three verses describing the form of the מן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The מן cannot be fully baked, unbaked dough, and raw grain all at once.

steps.title: The form depended on the person's level
steps.stepSummary: For צדיקים it came as bread, for בינונים as cakes, and for רשעים as grain they had to grind.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the righteous it came as bread; for average people it came as cakes; for the wicked, they had to grind it in a mill.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that each verse describes a different kind of person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The more righteous a person was, the less work the מן needed. A צדיק got it fully ready, a בינוני had to bake it, and a רשע had to grind and bake it. This matches the answer in Step 28 about how far each group had to go to collect it.
steps.whatToRemember: The מן showed each person's level: the more righteous, the easier it was, both in where it fell and how ready it was.

phrases.english: The righteous: bread,
average people: cakes,
the wicked: they ground it in a mill.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each verse refers to a different group of people
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All three verses describe the same מן for everyone, so they contradict.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each verse describes the מן as it came to a different spiritual level.

steps.title: Women's perfumes fell with the מן
steps.stepSummary: The words 'or beat it in a mortar' teach that women's perfumes, which are crushed in a mortar, fell together with the מן.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Or beat it in a mortar.' רבי יהודה said in the name of רב, and some say it was רבי חמא ברבי חנינא: This teaches that women's perfumes fell for Israel along with the מן, since that is something crushed in a mortar.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads another phrase of the same verse as a hint to an extra gift that came with the מן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מן itself did not need crushing, especially for the righteous, as we just learned. So the words 'beat it in a mortar' must point to something else that does get crushed: perfumes and fragrances for women.

keyTerms.meaning: Women's adornments; here, perfumes and fragrant spices
And some say (the statement is said by a different sage)

phrases.english: "Or beat it in a mortar":
Rabbi Yehuda said that Rav said,
and some say it was Rabbi Ḥama son of Rabbi Ḥanina:
This teaches that there fell for Israel
together with the manna women's perfumes,
something that is crushed in a mortar.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״אוֹ דָכוּ בַּמְּדוֹכָה״, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same verse (במדבר יא:ח) as Step 29, but now reads it as a hint to extra gifts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Women's perfumes fell together with the מן.

steps.title: Cooking spices fell with the מן
steps.stepSummary: The words 'and cooked it in a pot' teach that cooking spices fell with the מן.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And cooked it in a pot.' רבי חמא said: This teaches that cooking spices fell for Israel along with the מן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues with the next phrase of the verse and finds another extra gift in it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Same method as the step before. 'Cooking in a pot' hints to the seasonings people need to cook a dish, and these came down with the מן too.

keyTerms.meaning: Cooking spices, seasonings for the pot

phrases.english: "And cooked it in a pot":
Rabbi Ḥama said:
This teaches that there fell for Israel
together with the manna cooking spices.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel to Step 31, reading the next phrase of the same verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cooking spices fell together with the מן.

steps.title: What does 'every morning' mean for the donations?
steps.stepSummary: The verse says the people brought donations for the משכן 'every morning'. The גמרא asks why it says that.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And they brought him more free-will offerings every morning.' What does 'every morning' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a verse about donations for the משכן and asks about the strange words 'every morning'. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Donations do not have to be given in the morning, so the repeated phrase seems extra. The question suggests the phrase hints to something specific.

keyTerms.meaning: Every morning (literally: in the morning, in the morning)

phrases.english: "And they brought to him more free-will offerings
every morning."
What is "every morning"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new verse, but stays on the theme of gifts that fell with the מן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the verse stresses that the donations came 'every morning'.

steps.title: Precious stones fell with the מן
steps.stepSummary: They donated from what fell every morning, meaning precious stones and pearls came down with the מן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: They brought from the thing that fell for them 'every morning'. This teaches that precious stones and pearls fell for Israel along with the מן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'every morning' hints to where the donations came from: the things that fell each morning with the מן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מן fell every morning, and the phrase 'every morning' is used about the מן too. So the donations came from that morning delivery, which means precious stones and pearls fell with it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
From the thing that fell for them "every morning."
This teaches that there fell for Israel
precious stones and pearls together with the manna.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The donations came from the precious stones and pearls that fell each morning with the מן.

steps.title: Real clouds brought the onyx stones
steps.stepSummary: The verse says 'the נשיאים brought the onyx stones'. A ברייתא teaches that נשיאים here means real clouds.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And the נשיאים brought the onyx stones.' It was taught: real נשיאים, meaning actual clouds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a verse about the onyx stones for the כהן גדול's clothing and reads the word נשיאים in a new way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually נשיאים means the tribal leaders. Here the ברייתא says it means clouds, since the same word can mean clouds. So the clouds brought the stones down, which fits the idea that precious stones fell with the מן.

keyTerms.meaning: Onyx stones (used on the כהן גדול's shoulder pieces)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read נשיאים here as 'leaders'. The whole point is that it means clouds, which carried the stones down.

phrases.english: "And the nesi'im brought the onyx stones":
It was taught: actual clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds support to Step 34: the stones came from the sky.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word נשיאים in the verse means clouds, which brought the onyx stones.

steps.title: Proof that נשיאים can mean clouds
steps.stepSummary: A verse in משלי uses נשיאים next to wind and rain, showing that the word means clouds.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so it says: 'Clouds and wind, but no rain.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a verse to prove that the word נשיאים can mean clouds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In משלי, נשיאים appears together with wind and rain, so it clearly means clouds there. This supports reading the same word as 'clouds' in the verse about the onyx stones.

keyTerms.meaning: And so it says (introduces a supporting verse)

steps.whatToRemember: Along with the מן came extra gifts: perfumes, spices, and precious stones. The stones were used for the משכן and were brought down by the clouds.

phrases.english: And so it says:
"Clouds and wind, but no rain."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the reading given in Step 35.

steps.title: The מן tasted like a mother's milk
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו reads שד as 'breast': just as a baby tastes many flavors in milk, Israel found many flavors in the מן.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And its taste was like the taste of לשד השמן.' רבי אבהו said: Just as a baby tastes many flavors from the breast, so too the מן: whenever Israel ate it, they found many flavors in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the hard phrase 'לשד השמן' in the verse about the taste of the מן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבהו reads שד as 'breast'. A mother's milk changes taste based on what she eats, so a baby tastes many flavors. In the same way, the מן had many tastes for Israel.

phrases.english: "And its taste was like the taste of leshad hashamen."
Rabbi Abbahu said:
Just as with this breast, a baby
tastes in it many flavors,
so too the manna: whenever
Israel ate it,
they found in it many flavors.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: מָה שַׁד זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about the taste of the מן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מן had many different flavors, like a mother's milk.

steps.title: The מן changed like a shapeshifting demon
steps.stepSummary: Others read the word as שֵׁד (demon): just as a demon changes into many forms, the מן changed into many tastes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: it means an actual שֵׁד (demon). Just as a demon changes into many forms, so too the מן changed into many tastes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to read the same word, which reaches the same conclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of 'breast', this opinion reads the word as 'demon', which can change its appearance. The comparison is about changing: just as the demon changes form, the מן changed taste. Both readings agree that the מן had many tastes and differ only on the image.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say (a second version)

steps.whatToRemember: Both readings of 'לשד' teach the same thing: the מן changed its taste. One compares it to a mother's milk, the other to a demon that changes form.

phrases.english: There are those who say: literally a demon.

phrases.aramaic: מָה שֵׁד זֶה מִתְהַפֵּךְ לְכַמָּה גְּווֹנִין —
phrases.english: Just as this demon changes into many forms,
so too the manna changed into many flavors.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second reading of the same phrase explained in Step 37.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The מן changed into many tastes, like a demon changes into many forms.

steps.title: Meat requested improperly was given improperly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק about meat in the evening and bread in the morning. רבי יהושע בן קרחה teaches that because the people asked for meat improperly, it was given to them improperly.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And משה said: when ה' gives you meat to eat in the evening, and bread in the morning to be satisfied.' A ברייתא taught in the name of רבי יהושע בן קרחה: the meat, which they asked for improperly, was given to them improperly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new פסוק and a ברייתא that explains why the meat and the bread were given differently. This is the first half of the explanation. The second half, about the bread, continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The people already had the מן, so asking for meat was a complaint, not a real need. The פסוק describes the two foods differently. The meat comes 'in the evening' and only 'to eat,' while the bread comes 'in the morning' and 'to be satisfied.' רבי יהושע בן קרחה reads this difference as a hint that the meat came in a less favorable way, because the request for it was improper.

keyTerms.meaning: Improperly, not in the fitting way
To be satisfied, to eat one's fill

steps.confusionAlert: This is only half of רבי יהושע בן קרחה's statement. Don't think the teaching is finished. It sets up a contrast with the bread (the מן), which was requested properly and is explained on the next amud.
steps.whyThisMatters: It introduces a principle that ties how something is asked for to how it is given. The גמרא will build on this as it continues explaining the details of the מן.

phrases.english: "And Moses said: when the Lord gives you
in the evening meat to eat
and bread in the morning to be satisfied"
phrases.notes: Bread: morning, and 'to be satisfied'. This is the contrast the ברייתא builds on.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה:
phrases.english: It was taught in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha:
The meat which they asked for improperly
phrases.notes: They already had the מן, so they did not truly need meat

phrases.english: was given to them improperly,
phrases.notes: The statement continues on the next amud, about the bread

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the aggadic discussion of the מן. After explaining its many tastes, the גמרא now looks at how the meat and the bread were given.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat that was requested improperly was given in an improper, less favorable manner, as hinted by the wording of the פסוק (evening, 'to eat').
